title.en: Confucius and the True Sage in the West (Liezi)
title.zh: 西方之人有聖者焉（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: The court of the Shang minister (symbolic pin: Anyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 商太宰之廷（象徵定位：河南安陽）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: A high official from Shang quizzes Confucius on the sages — the Three Kings, Five Emperors, Three Sovereigns — and gets the same 'I do not know that they were sages.' Confucius changes countenance: among the people of the West a true sage dwells — he governs not, yet there is no disorder; he speaks not, yet he is naturally trusted; so great and incomprehensible is he that the people can find no name to call him by.
summary.zh: 商太宰問於孔子：三王、五帝、三皇皆聖乎？孔子曰：西方之人有聖者焉——不治而不亂，不言而自信，不化而自行，蕩蕩乎民無能名焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'true sage in the West' passage later attracted the Jesuit reading as an allusion to Christ. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A high official from Shang paid a visit to Confucius. "You are a sage, are you not?" he inquired. "A sage!" replied Confucius. "How could I venture to think so? I am only a man of extensive learning and moral culture." The Minister then asked: "Were the Three Kings sages?" "The Three Kings," replied Confucius, "were great in the exercise of wisdom and courage. I do not know, however, that they were sages." "What of the Five Emperors? Were they not sages?" "The Five Emperors excelled in the exercise of altruism and righteousness. I do not know that they were sages." "And the Three Sovereigns: surely they were sages?" "The Three Sovereigns excelled in the virtues that were suited to their age. But whether they were sages or no I really cannot say."

The expression of Confucius' countenance changed, and he replied after a pause: "Among the people of the West a true sage dwells. He governs not, yet there is no disorder. He speaks not, yet he is naturally trusted. He makes no reforms, yet right conduct is spontaneous and universal. So great and incomprehensible is he that the people can find no name to call him by. I suspect that this man is a sage, but whether in truth he is a sage or is not a sage I do not know." The Minister from Shang meditated awhile in silence. Then he said to himself: "Confucius is making a fool of me!"

title.zh: 南郭子貌陋而心虛（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: Nan-kuo, Lieh Tzŭ's neighbourhood (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Nan-kuo Tzŭ, Lieh Tzŭ's next-door neighbour of twenty years with whom no visit passed, turns out to be a repulsive-looking creature who gazes blankly, body and soul seeming not to belong together — yet he fraternises with the hindmost row of disciples. He who has reached the stage of thought is silent; he who uses silence in lieu of speech really does speak.
summary.zh: 子列子學於壺丘子林——南郭子貌陋，形若槁木；迎見而語——見同者形骸之外，不以鏡之於形骸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Nan-kuo Tzu was his next-door neighbour, but for twenty years no visit passed between them, and when they met in the street they made as though they had not seen each other. ... Accordingly, forty of the disciples went with him to call on Nan-kuo Tzu, who turned out to be a repulsive-looking creature. He made no show of receiving his guests, but only gazed blankly at Lieh Tzu. Body and soul seemed not to belong together, and to be unable to respond to the stimuli of the external world.

Their Master Lieh Tzu said to them: "He who has reached the stage of thought is silent. He who has attained to perfect knowledge is also silent. He who uses silence in lieu of speech really does speak. He who for knowledge substitutes blankness of mind really does know. Without words and speaking not, without knowledge and knowing not, he really speaks and really knows. Saying nothing and knowing nothing, there is in reality nothing that he does not say, nothing that he does not know."

title.en: Lung Shu's Hollow Square Inch of Heart (Liezi)
title.zh: 龍叔謂文摯：心有七孔（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: The physician's chamber (symbolic pin: Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 文摯之室（象徵定位：山東臨淄）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Lung Shu tells the master of cunning arts that praise and disgrace, gain and loss, life and death, riches and poverty excite him nothing — what disease is this? Wen Chih, facing the light, sees that a good square inch of Lung Shu's heart is hollow, six of its orifices open and only the seventh blocked: you are mistaking for a disease that which is really divine enlightenment.
summary.zh: 龍叔謂文摯曰：吾疾——譽不以為榮，毀不以為辱；得而不喜，失而弗憂——文摯曰：見子之心矣，方寸之地虛矣；幾聖人也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "I hold it no honour," said Lung Shu, "to be praised in my native village, nor do I consider it a disgrace to be decried in my native State. Gain excites in me no joy, and loss no sorrow. I look upon life in the same light as death, upon riches in the same light as poverty, upon my fellow-men as so many swine, and upon myself as I look upon my fellow-men. I dwell in my home as though it were a mere caravanserai, and regard my native district with no more feeling than I would a barbarian State. Afflicted as I am in these various ways, honours and rewards fail to rouse me, pains and penalties to overawe me, good or bad fortune to influence me, joy or grief to move me."

Wen Chih replied by asking Lung Shu to stand with his back to the light, while he himself faced the light and looked at him intently. "Ah!" said he after a while, "I see that a good square inch of your heart is hollow. You are within an ace of being a true sage. Six of the orifices in your heart are open and clear, and only the seventh is blocked up. This, however, is doubtless due to the fact that you are mistaking for a disease that which is really divine enlightenment. It is a case in which my shallow art is of no avail."

title.en: Teng Hsi's Herd of Swine and the Retort of the Vassals (Liezi)
title.zh: 鄧析難伯豐子，如犬彘乎（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: Tung-li, in the Chêng State (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Teng Hsi the sophist greets the vassals of Po Feng Tzu with the sneer that those who receive sustenance from others through inability to support themselves are in the category of dogs and swine. One of the company retorts: it is really we who may be said to employ the Government authorities — only when there is a combination of technical knowledge and power can co-operative service exist. Teng Hsi could think of nothing to say in reply.
summary.zh: 鄧析顧其徒曰：為若受——子不能自給，受養於人，犬豕之類也。伯豐子之從者曰：齊楚之處士多為工焉——吾實謂役使君之臣者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Teng Hsi then turned to Po Feng Tzu. "Are you acquainted with the true theory of Sustentation?" he inquired. "To receive sustenance from others, through inability to support oneself, places one in the category of dogs and swine. It is man's prerogative to give sustenance to other creatures, and to use them for his own purposes. That you and your fellows are provided with abundant food and comfortable clothing is due to the Government. Young and old, you herd together, and are penned up like cattle destined for the shambles: in what respect are you to be distinguished from dogs and swine?"

One of his company, disregarding the rules of precedence, stepped forward and said: "Has your Excellency never heard of the variety of craftsmen in Ch'i and Lu? Some are skilled potters and carpenters, others are clever workers in metal and leather; there are good musicians, trained scribes and accountants, military experts and men learned in the ritual of ancestor-worship. All kinds of craftsmanship are there fully represented. Now, if there were no division of ranks and duties, mutual co-operation would be impossible. ... It is really we who may be said to employ the Government authorities. Why then should you pity us?" Teng Hsi could think of nothing to say in reply.
